Chapter Four: The Limits of Help and the Struggle with Institutions
When you live in the projects, you’re told that help is out there—maybe from schools, social workers, or government programs. But let’s be honest, most of the time, these systems just don’t measure up.
The boys’ mom? She spends hours on end filling out forms, standing in lines, and sitting through meetings with officials who seem to care more about the rules than the people right in front of them. She wants so badly to do right by her kids, but every step forward feels like another hurdle.
School is supposed to be the place where things get better, right? But for these boys, the challenges go way beyond textbooks and homework. Teachers are stretched thin, there’s never enough to go around, and the school building itself is falling apart. The older brother tries to keep up, but when you feel invisible, it’s tough to stay motivated. The younger one? Sometimes he acts out—not because he doesn’t care, but because he’s frustrated by a system that seems to have forgotten him.
They both know education matters. Still, it’s hard to buy into that dream when you’re constantly reminded that the odds just aren’t in your favor.
Now, let’s talk about social services. They’re supposed to be a safety net, but for this family, that net is full of holes. They wait and wait—for food stamps, for someone to fix what’s broken in their apartment, for help that arrives too late, or sometimes, not at all. The mother feels like she’s being judged, as if needing help is somehow her own fault, not just a tough hand she’s been dealt. She keeps pushing forward, but you can hear the exhaustion in her voice.
The boys see all of this firsthand. They watch neighbors get evicted, friends slip through the cracks, and they hear promises that never seem to materialize. Pretty soon, they start to realize: depending on institutions can be a gamble. Sometimes, it’s safer to lean on family or friends.
Despite everything, they hang on to hope—a hope that maybe, just maybe, the system will see them for who they are, not just another number on a form.
What becomes clear is this: the real failure isn’t just the paperwork or the endless waiting—it’s a failure of trust. When help is inconsistent or nearly impossible to get, people start to lose faith that things will ever get better.
And yet, the boys’ family keeps trying. They find little pockets of support—a teacher who actually listens, a neighbor who shares what little they have, a community group that opens its doors and offers a safe spot to land.
Over the years, these boys learn how to navigate all the red tape. They become experts at reading between the lines, figuring out how to get around obstacles, and standing up for each other. Their resilience is nothing short of remarkable. But it’s also a stark reminder—just think about how much more is expected from those who have the least.
In the end, their story isn’t just about struggling with poverty. It’s about how society can fail its most vulnerable—and the quiet, steady determination of people who, despite it all, refuse to give up.
